{{Citation}}
[[File:DevastatorTantiveIV.png|thumb|right|250px|The ion drives of an [[Imperial I-class Star Destroyer/Legends|''Imperial''-class Star Destroyer]]]]
The '''ion engine''' or '''ion drive''' was a type of engine used to propel most [[Starship/Legends|starships]] at [[Sublight engine/Legends|sublight]] velocities. Ion engines were fueled by power cells, liquid chemical reactants, onboard generators, or virtually any other device capable of providing sufficient power. The engine utilized internal [[Nuclear fusion|fusion reactions]] to produce a stream of highly charged particles that were forced through the engine's exhaust port at nearly the speed of light. Ion engines were sometimes called '''ion rockets'''.

Ion engines emitted mildly [[Radiation/Legends|radioactive]] byproducts, requiring onboard technicians to wear protective gear. Because of this radioactivity, and the disabling effects that ions had on electronics and electrical systems, it was common protocol for most ships to utilize [[Repulsorlift/Legends|repulsorlifts]] for propulsion during atmospheric flight and reserve use of the more powerful ion drives for orbital navigation.

The most noted craft using ion drives were [[TIE/ln space superiority starfighter/Legends|TIE fighters]], which received their name from the number of ion engines they used: '''T'''win '''I'''on '''E'''ngine.

==Behind the scenes==
Ion drives are becoming real devices as the first successful test of the [[Wikipedia:Dawn (spacecraft)|''Dawn'' spacecraft's]] ion engines used [[Wikipedia:Xenon|Xenon]] propellant. It burned for 27 hours and only expended 10 ounces of fuel.<ref name="JPL">{{WebCite|url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.cfm?release=2007-115|text=Dawn Mission Status: Spacecraft Tests Ion Engine|date=2007-10-09|work=NASA|archivedate=20071011073340}}</ref> Real ion thrusters look very similar to the engines on Star Destroyers. However, they have a very low thrust-to-weight ratio; this problem is fixed with the introduction of very similar ''plasma engines'', which have a variable and scalable thrust-to-weight ratio.
